passage:
The claims clerk at the NGO's Nashik field office wanted travel forms by five.
Uma's July form had one line she kept looking at: "Auto to Sinnar village, ₹350." She had gone by bus. Forty rupees. Her phone bill was overdue, and salary was nine days away.
I'll adjust it next month, she thought. It's basically borrowing.
Jaya, filling in her own form at the next desk, didn't even look up. "Everyone rounds up the field trips. They budget for it."
Uma signed. The clerk stamped it without a glance.
In August she didn't adjust anything. She wrote "Auto, ₹350" for two trips she had taken by bus, and noticed, with a strange flatness, that her hand hadn't paused at all this time. It was just a form now.
On the bus home that evening she looked out of the window and tried to remember when it had stopped feeling like anything.

qa.q: How much did Uma's bus trip to Sinnar actually cost?
qa.a: Uma's bus trip cost forty rupees.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when she signed the July form?
qa.a: Uma felt uneasy, her eyes going back to that line, but calmed herself by saying it was basically borrowing she would adjust next month.

qa.q: At which moment could Uma most easily have stopped, and how?
qa.a: In July, before signing, Uma could have corrected the line to the real bus fare; after the first time, the next step felt much easier.

qa.q: How might Jaya's remark have affected Uma's choice?
qa.a: Jaya's "everyone rounds up" made the claim sound normal, giving Uma one more excuse at the exact moment she was unsure.

grounding: An employee pads a travel claim thinking she will fix it next month and that everyone does it, and finds the second time takes no effort at all.

passage:
Dear Sharmila Ma'am,
You trained me in my first year, so I'm writing to you because I can't say this to anyone at work.
In March I was two orders short of my quarter target. A client had promised an order for April. I entered it as a March sale. Only a date. I told myself I'd correct it in April, and that everyone on the floor does it at quarter-end.
April came and I didn't correct it. I was short again in June, and this time I moved two orders without even thinking about it for long.
That's what scares me. The first time my hands were cold. The second time I was eating lunch.
I don't feel like a dishonest person. I think that's the problem.
Could I call you on Sunday? I want to fix this before it becomes the way I work.
Sangeeta

qa.q: How many orders did Sangeeta move in June?
qa.a: Sangeeta moved two orders in June.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta find the second time more frightening than the first?
qa.a: The first time Sangeeta's hands were cold, but the second time it barely took a thought, so Sangeeta is scared by how easy it has become.

qa.q: What is the wise step Sangeeta takes by writing this letter?
qa.a: Sangeeta reaches out to a trusted senior and asks to talk on Sunday, aiming to fix things before the habit becomes a way of working.

qa.q: How might Sharmila Ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sharmila Ma'am might be worried but also moved that someone Sharmila Ma'am trained is being honest about it and asking for help early.

grounding: Sangeeta books a future order early, with the excuses of fixing it later and everyone doing it, and finds the second step far easier than the first.

passage:
On the last Friday of the quarter, Daniel sat alone in the Stockholm office, looking at one cell in the sales report. His team was a little short of target. If one client's order went in today instead of next week, the number would turn green. That morning Anders, his manager, had said, "We can't miss again."
It's borrowing, Daniel told himself. The order is real. It's only a few days early. I'll fix it next quarter. Everyone smooths the edges a little.
He typed the date. The cell turned green. He felt a small lift of relief, then a queasy weight, like a stone in his pocket.
At dinner he laughed a little too loudly at his partner's story. Later he lay awake, working out how next quarter would now need to be even better, to cover this one.

qa.q: What did Anders say that morning?
qa.a: 'We can't miss again.'

qa.q: What did Daniel feel after the cell turned green?
qa.a: Daniel felt a small lift of relief, then a queasy weight like a stone in his pocket, the start of guilt.

qa.q: What could Daniel do on Monday before it grows?
qa.a: Put the date back and tell Anders the team is short, accepting a missed target now instead of a bigger gap next quarter.

qa.q: How might Anders see the green number?
qa.a: Anders would see the target met and relax, not knowing the number was borrowed, which makes the pressure worse next quarter.

grounding: Shows an employee fudging one number under target pressure, calling it borrowing, and already feeling how it makes the next step likelier.

passage:
In the accounts room of the engineering college, Damini filled in her travel claim for the inspection visit. The auto had cost very little. The form had a box for "taxi".
"Just put taxi," Chinmay said from the next desk, not looking up. "Everyone does. They pay us nothing anyway."
Damini's pen hovered. Her brother's coaching fees were due. It's only this once, she thought. It's not really stealing; the college owes me for all the Saturdays I've worked. I'll make it up somehow.
She ticked "taxi" and wrote a round figure. Her hand felt strange, as if it belonged to someone else.
The claim was approved in two days, no questions asked. The second time, a month later, she didn't even pause. That surprised her more than anything.

qa.q: Which box did Damini tick on the travel claim?
qa.a: She ticked 'taxi'.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as the pen hovered?
qa.a: Damini felt pressured by her brother's fees and uneasy, telling herself it was only once and that the college owed her for the Saturdays.

qa.q: What could Damini do now that a second claim has gone through?
qa.a: Stop, correct both claims with accounts, and speak to a trusted senior before the habit grows.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see small padding of claims?
qa.a: Chinmay treats it as normal, 'Everyone does', which made Damini's first step feel easier than it should have.

grounding: Shows an employee padding one expense claim with 'everyone does it', and finding the second time needed no pause at all.

passage:
Dear Harsha anna,
I'm writing this instead of calling because I can't say it out loud yet.
At the pharmacy, the stock count was short last month. Just a little. I think one of the new boys miscounted. If I reported it, the area manager would come, there'd be questions, maybe my bonus would go. So I adjusted the register to match. One line. I told myself I'd find the missing stock next month and put it right.
This month it was short again. Adjusting it was easier this time. That's what scares me. The first time my hands were shaking. The second time I was humming.
I keep calling it "borrowing time". I'm not a thief, anna. You know me. But I don't like how easy it's getting.
Can we talk on Sunday?
Nirmala

qa.q: What did Nirmala do when the stock count was short?
qa.a: Nirmala adjusted the register to match. One line.

qa.q: Why does the second adjustment scare Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala feels frightened that it was easier the second time, humming instead of shaking, which shows how the first step smooths the next.

qa.q: What would be a wise next step for Nirmala?
qa.a: Talk to Harsha anna on Sunday, then report the shortages and the adjustments to the area manager before the gap grows.

qa.q: How might Harsha anna feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Harsha anna would likely feel worried but trusted, since Nirmala chose to confide before it went further.

grounding: Shows an employee adjusting a record to cover a shortfall, calling it borrowing time, and noticing the second step came easier.

passage: Irfan, you know me as the rule-follower, right? So listen. Last year, when Amma's hospital bills came in, I was short at the end of the month. I had a client trip to Coimbatore. The taxi was four hundred; on the claim form I wrote seven hundred. I told myself it was borrowing. I'd work extra and put it back somehow, next month. And honestly, in our office everyone rounds up. That's what I kept saying: everyone does it. The strange part is how easy the second time was. And the third. My hand didn't even hesitate. By March I had a little ledger in my head of what I owed the company, and it kept growing. Then our new manager said casually, "We're doing a sample audit of travel claims." My whole body went cold. That night I couldn't sleep. It wasn't the audit. It was realising that I, Kalyani, had become someone who needed an audit to stop. The next morning I asked to meet her.

qa.q: What did the taxi actually cost, and what did Kalyani claim?
qa.a: The taxi was four hundred; Kalyani wrote seven hundred.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the audit was announced?
qa.a: Kalyani went cold with fear, and that night felt shaken to see how far the so-called borrowing had gone.

qa.q: What turning point could stop the slide, and what should Kalyani do?
qa.a: Asking to meet the manager the next morning; Kalyani should tell the truth, correct the claims and put the money back, before being found out.

qa.q: How might colleagues who round up see it if they heard this?
qa.a: They might feel uneasy, recognising how everyone does it makes a first small step feel normal and later ones easier.

grounding: Shows an employee who fudges an expense, calling it borrowing and telling themselves everyone does it, and finds each later step easier.
